purpose: Recognize the bacteria and viruses most often linked to produce outbreaks and know where each one comes from, so you can tell which practices protect against which hazard.

blocks.text: Two kinds of hazards, two kinds of sources

text: The microbes that cause produce outbreaks fall into two groups. **Bacteria** mostly come from animal feces and the environment. **Viruses** mostly come from people, especially workers who handle produce while sick.

blocks.caption: Pathogens linked to fresh produce and where they come from
rows: Feces from cattle and other animals, carried by water, manure, or wildlife
Feces from animals including birds and reptiles; contaminated water
Soil and damp packing areas; it can grow in cool, wet places
Sick workers, through hands and poor handwashing
Infected workers, sometimes before they feel ill

blocks.label: Key idea
text: Match the control to the source. Water and manure practices target bacteria. Worker health and handwashing practices target viruses.

cards.front: Which pathogen can grow in a cool, damp packing shed?
back: Listeria monocytogenes. It survives and grows in cool, wet environments, which is why packing area sanitation matters.

cards.front: Where do norovirus and hepatitis A usually come from on a farm?
back: People. Sick or infected workers transfer them through their hands.

questions.stem: A worker had vomiting last night and feels better this morning. Which hazard is the main concern if they harvest lettuce today?
questions.rationale: Norovirus spreads from people and stays infectious after symptoms end. The other two come from the environment, not from this worker.

text: Which of these sources is present on your farm right now: livestock, wildlife, a pond, a packing shed, or seasonal workers?
